content: Aloe vera, also known as Aloe barbadensis or Aloe vulgaris Lam., is a species of the Aloe genus that originates from northern Africa. It is a succulent plant that is either stemless or has a very short stem, growing to a height of 80–100 cm. The plant propagates through offsets and root sprouts. Its leaves are lanceolate in shape, thick, fleshy, and range in color from green to gray-green, with serrated edges. The flowers are borne on spikes that can grow up to 90 cm tall. Each flower is pendulous and features a yellow tubular corolla measuring 2–3 cm in length. Cultivation Aloe vera is relatively easy to cultivate in frost-free climates. It thrives in well-drained, sandy potting soil and moderate light conditions. A high-quality commercial potting mix, supplemented with additional perlite, granite grit, or coarse sand, is recommended for optimal growth. Alternatively, pre-packaged cacti and succulent mixes can also be used. Potted plants should be allowed to dry out completely before re-watering. During winter, Aloe vera may enter a dormant phase, requiring minimal moisture. In regions with frost or snow, the plant is best kept indoors or in heated greenhouses. Aloe vera has been cultivated for centuries in arid tropical and subtropical regions, both as an ornamental plant and for its use in herbal medicine. For more information on its medicinal properties, refer to related Aloe species. Food Preservation Researchers at the University of Miguel Hernández in Alicante, Spain, have developed a gel derived from Aloe vera that extends the shelf life of fresh produce, such as fruits and vegetables. This gel is tasteless, colorless, and odorless, making it a safe and environmentally friendly alternative to synthetic preservatives like sulfur dioxide. Studies have demonstrated that grapes stored at 1°C and coated with this gel could be preserved for 35 days, compared to only 7 days for untreated grapes. The gel forms a protective barrier against oxygen and moisture in the air and inhibits the activity of microorganisms responsible for foodborne illnesses through its antibiotic and antifungal properties. Medicinal Uses Aloe vera has been traditionally used externally to treat various skin conditions, including cuts, burns, and eczema. The sap of Aloe vera is believed to alleviate pain and reduce inflammation. However, evidence regarding its effects on wound healing is contradictory. A study conducted in the 1990s found that moderate to severe burns healed faster when treated regularly with Aloe vera gel compared to wounds covered with gauze bandages. Conversely, another study suggested that wounds treated with Aloe vera gel healed more slowly. The plant's beneficial properties are thought to be due to mucopolysaccharides, particularly acemannan, found in the inner gel of the leaf. An injectable form of acemannan, marketed as Acemannan Immunostimulant™ by Carrington Laboratories, has been approved in the United States for treating fibrosarcoma (a type of cancer) in dogs and cats following clinical trials. However, it is not approved for human use and is only available through veterinary prescription. Cosmetic companies frequently incorporate Aloe vera sap or derivatives into products such as makeup, moisturizers, soaps, sunscreens, shampoos, and lotions, although the effectiveness of Aloe vera in these products remains uncertain. Aloe vera gel is also claimed to be beneficial for dry skin conditions, particularly eczema around the eyes and sensitive facial skin. An article in the British Journal of General Practice suggests that Aloe vera is effective in treating athlete's foot. While there are promising results, the clinical effectiveness of oral or topical Aloe vera for wound healing and other uses remains unclear. Aloe vera juice may provide relief for some individuals with ulcerative colitis, an inflammatory bowel disease. Parts Used The lower leaf of the Aloe vera plant is commonly used for medicinal purposes. When sliced open, the gel obtained from the leaf can be applied directly to affected areas of the skin. Both the leaves and seeds of Aloe vera are edible. Use in Foods In Japan, Aloe vera is a common ingredient in commercially available yogurt. Many companies also produce Aloe vera-based beverages. In Pakistan, the plant has been used for centuries as a carminative and digestive aid. The dried gel is mixed with seeds of various herbs and consumed after meals. In the Hazara region of Pakistan's North West Frontier Province, Pashtuns have used Aloe vera for centuries to enhance physical endurance, likely due to the gel's high nutrient content. In Rajasthan, India, Aloe vera is prepared as a vegetable dish with fenugreek seeds. In Tamil Nadu, India, it is used to make a curry served with Indian bread or rice. Popular beverages, such as SoBe's Strawberry Daiquirí, also contain Aloe vera. In Mexico, Aloe vera smoothies are commonly consumed.
